lessonTitle: Gluconeogenesis and Glycogen Metabolism: Making and Storing Glucose

blocks.text: At about kilometre 32 of a marathon, a runner suddenly slows, feels weak and confused, and describes 'hitting the wall'. Muscle and liver glycogen are nearly exhausted, and the brain, which cannot burn fatty acids, now depends on glucose the body must manufacture. This unit explains how the body stores glucose as glycogen and how it builds new glucose when stores run low.

blocks.markdown:
**Why glucose must be made as well as stored.** The brain and red blood cells need a steady supply of glucose (the brain normally uses roughly 100 to 120 g per day). Liver glycogen, the only store that can release glucose into the blood, holds only enough to cover roughly a day of fasting at most, and less with exertion. After that, the liver (and, in prolonged fasting, the kidney cortex) makes glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors by **gluconeogenesis**.

The main substrates are: **lactate** (from red cells and exercising muscle, the Cori cycle), **glycerol** (from the breakdown of triacylglycerol in adipose tissue), and **glucogenic amino acids** such as alanine (from muscle protein breakdown). **Even-chain fatty acids cannot be converted to a net gain of glucose in humans**: their product, acetyl-CoA, loses both of its carbons as CO2 in the citric acid cycle before oxaloacetate is regenerated, so there is no net carbon for glucose. Glycerol, however, can be used because it enters at the level of triose phosphate.

blocks.title: Gluconeogenesis
blocks.text: Gluconeogenesis is the synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors (lactate, glycerol, glucogenic amino acids). It occurs mainly in the liver and, to a lesser extent, the kidney cortex. It is not simply glycolysis run backwards: three glycolytic steps are so energetically downhill that they cannot be reversed, and each is bypassed by a different enzyme.

blocks.markdown: **Bypassing the three irreversible steps.** Glycolysis contains three reactions with large negative free-energy change: hexokinase/glucokinase (glucose to glucose-6-phosphate), phosphofructokinase-1 (fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate) and pyruvate kinase (phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate). The seven near-equilibrium glycolytic reactions run in either direction, so gluconeogenesis uses them in reverse. Only the three irreversible steps need separate enzymes. The pyruvate kinase step is bypassed in two stages: pyruvate carboxylase (a **mitochondrial** enzyme needing **biotin**, ATP and CO2) makes oxaloacetate, and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK) converts oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate using GTP and releasing CO2.

rows: Acetyl-CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase; glucagon induces PEPCK
Inhibited by fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and AMP; activated by citrate
blocks.caption: Each irreversible glycolytic step has a separate gluconeogenic bypass. Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (high when insulin is high) activates PFK-1 and inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, so the two pathways are not active at the same time.

blocks.title: Energy cost of making one glucose from pyruvate
blocks.prompt: Count the high-energy phosphate bonds spent in converting two molecules of pyruvate into one molecule of glucose in the liver.

steps.text: Pyruvate carboxylase: pyruvate + CO2 + ATP gives oxaloacetate. This occurs twice (two pyruvate), costing 2 ATP.
PEPCK: oxaloacetate + GTP gives phosphoenolpyruvate + CO2. Twice, costing 2 GTP (equivalent to 2 ATP).
Reverse of phosphoglycerate kinase: 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate is made from 3-phosphoglycerate using ATP. There are two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate, costing 2 ATP.
The other bypasses (fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, glucose-6-phosphatase) are hydrolyses that release phosphate and cost no ATP. Total = 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 high-energy phosphate bonds (4 ATP and 2 GTP).

blocks.answer: Six high-energy phosphate bonds (4 ATP + 2 GTP) are consumed, in addition to 2 NADH used in the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase reaction run in reverse.

blocks.caption: Overall stoichiometry of gluconeogenesis from pyruvate. By contrast glycolysis of one glucose yields only a net 2 ATP, so the pathway is energetically expensive and is switched on only when fuel is scarce.

blocks.markdown:
**Glycogen structure and synthesis.** Glycogen is a branched polymer of glucose: chains joined by **alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds**, with **alpha-1,6 branches** roughly every 8 to 12 residues. Branching makes it highly soluble and gives many chain ends for rapid release. Synthesis begins on the protein primer **glycogenin**. Glucose-6-phosphate is converted to glucose-1-phosphate (phosphoglucomutase), then to **UDP-glucose** (UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase). **Glycogen synthase** (the regulated step) adds glucose to the non-reducing ends by alpha-1,4 bonds, and the **branching enzyme** moves a block of about 7 residues to make an alpha-1,6 link.

**Breakdown (glycogenolysis).** **Glycogen phosphorylase** (cofactor pyridoxal phosphate) cleaves alpha-1,4 bonds by phosphorolysis, releasing glucose-1-phosphate, until four residues remain before a branch. The **debranching enzyme** (a transferase that moves three residues and an alpha-1,6-glucosidase that releases the branch-point glucose as free glucose) then clears the branch. Glucose-1-phosphate becomes glucose-6-phosphate. Only the **liver** (and kidney) contains **glucose-6-phosphatase**, so only liver glycogen can supply blood glucose; muscle uses its glucose-6-phosphate internally for glycolysis.

rows: Gs, adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, protein kinase A
cAMP (beta receptor); in liver also Ca2+ (alpha-1)
Breakdown; muscle also rises with Ca2+ and AMP during contraction
blocks.caption: Hormonal control of glycogen metabolism. Glucagon acts on the liver only; muscle lacks glucagon receptors.

blocks.title: How long can liver glycogen sustain the blood glucose?
blocks.prompt: A fasting adult has 100 g of liver glycogen. The brain and red cells use glucose at 5 g per hour in total, and gluconeogenesis supplies 1 g per hour of this. Estimate how many hours the liver glycogen lasts.

steps.text: Total glucose demand = 5 g per hour.
Gluconeogenesis covers 1 g per hour, so glycogenolysis must supply 5 - 1 = 4 g per hour.
Time = store divided by rate = 100 g / 4 g per hour = 25 hours.

blocks.answer: About 25 hours. In reality, exercise or illness raises demand and the store empties sooner, and gluconeogenesis takes over an increasing share as fasting continues.

rows: Severe fasting hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia, hyperlipidaemia; glucagon does not raise blood glucose
Glycogen accumulates in lysosomes; cardiomegaly and hypotonia in infants; blood glucose normal
Hepatomegaly and fasting hypoglycaemia (milder than type I), abnormal glycogen with short outer branches; gluconeogenesis intact so no marked lactic acidosis
Exercise intolerance, cramps, myoglobinuria; ischaemic forearm exercise does not raise venous lactate; no hypoglycaemia
blocks.caption: Glycogen storage diseases: the tissue where the enzyme is expressed explains whether the problem is hypoglycaemia (liver) or exercise intolerance (muscle).

items: Ask which tissue is affected: hepatomegaly and fasting hypoglycaemia point to a liver enzyme, exercise cramps with myoglobinuria point to muscle.

If glucose-6-phosphate cannot be dephosphorylated (type I), it accumulates, diverts into glycolysis and gives lactate, and the same block prevents gluconeogenesis from releasing glucose, so lactate and uric acid rise.
If the debranching enzyme is missing (type III), glycogen can only be broken down to the branch points, so some glucose can still be released but not all.
If muscle phosphorylase is missing (type V), glycogen cannot supply glycolysis during exercise, so lactate does not rise and energy is short.

blocks.title: Reciprocal regulation prevents a futile cycle
blocks.text: In the fasting liver, glucagon raises cAMP, which activates phosphorylase, inactivates glycogen synthase, and lowers fructose-2,6-bisphosphate. This favours gluconeogenesis and glycogen breakdown while shutting down glycolysis and glycogen synthesis. Insulin does the reverse. Acetyl-CoA from fatty acid oxidation also activates pyruvate carboxylase, linking fat breakdown to glucose production.

blocks.title: Muscle cannot release glucose
blocks.text: Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase and glucagon receptors, so muscle glycogen is a private fuel store. It supports blood glucose only indirectly, via lactate and alanine that travel to the liver.

points: Gluconeogenesis makes glucose from lactate, glycerol and glucogenic amino acids using three bypass enzymes: pyruvate carboxylase with PEPCK, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and glucose-6-phosphatase.

Glycogen is synthesised by glycogen synthase and the branching enzyme and broken down by phosphorylase and the debranching enzyme; glucagon and adrenaline drive breakdown through cAMP, insulin drives synthesis.
Only the liver can export glucose from glycogen because only the liver has glucose-6-phosphatase.
Glycogen storage diseases are explained by which enzyme is missing and in which tissue: liver defects cause hypoglycaemia, muscle defects cause exercise intolerance.

questions.stem: Which enzyme converts oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate in gluconeogenesis?

distractorRationale.a: Pyruvate carboxylase makes oxaloacetate from pyruvate, the step before PEPCK, rather than making phosphoenolpyruvate.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: PEPCK decarboxylates and phosphorylates oxaloacetate using GTP to give phosphoenolpyruvate.
distractorRationale.c: Pyruvate kinase catalyses the reverse, irreversible glycolytic reaction (phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate).
distractorRationale.d: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase bypasses PFK-1 further along the pathway and acts on a sugar bisphosphate.

questions.explanation: Gluconeogenesis bypasses pyruvate kinase in two stages: pyruvate carboxylase forms oxaloacetate in the mitochondrion, then PEPCK converts oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate using GTP and releasing CO2. PEPCK is therefore the enzyme that produces phosphoenolpyruvate.

questions.stem: During prolonged fasting, rapid hepatic fatty acid oxidation raises the concentration of acetyl-CoA in liver mitochondria. What is the effect of this on gluconeogenesis?

options.text: It is converted directly to net glucose

distractorRationale.a: Correct: acetyl-CoA is the allosteric activator of pyruvate carboxylase, coupling fat oxidation to glucose production.
distractorRationale.b: Inhibition would shut down gluconeogenesis just when fuel is scarce; the regulation runs the other way.
distractorRationale.c: Glycogen synthase is controlled by phosphorylation, not acetyl-CoA, and fasting inactivates it.
distractorRationale.d: Acetyl-CoA loses both carbons as CO2 in the citric acid cycle, so it cannot give net glucose.

questions.explanation: Acetyl-CoA allosterically activates pyruvate carboxylase, so a high acetyl-CoA level signals that fatty acids are the main fuel and that oxaloacetate should be made for gluconeogenesis. It does not itself become glucose, because its two carbons are lost as CO2 in the cycle.

questions.stem: In a fasting hepatocyte, glucagon binds its receptor and raises cAMP. What is the resulting state of glycogen synthase and glycogen phosphorylase?

options.text: Synthase phosphorylated and inactive; phosphorylase phosphorylated and active
Synthase dephosphorylated and active; phosphorylase phosphorylated and active
Synthase phosphorylated and inactive; phosphorylase dephosphorylated and inactive
Synthase dephosphorylated and active; phosphorylase dephosphorylated and inactive

questions.correctOptionText: Synthase phosphorylated and inactive; phosphorylase phosphorylated and active

distractorRationale.a: Correct: protein kinase A and phosphorylase kinase phosphorylate synthase (inactivating it) and phosphorylase (activating it).
distractorRationale.b: Active synthase and active phosphorylase together would create a futile cycle; synthase is inactivated by phosphorylation.
distractorRationale.c: Phosphorylation activates, not inactivates, phosphorylase, so this describes the state in which glycogen cannot be broken down.
distractorRationale.d: This is the insulin (fed) pattern, not the glucagon pattern.

questions.explanation: Glucagon raises cAMP, which activates protein kinase A; this phosphorylates phosphorylase kinase (which then activates phosphorylase) and phosphorylates glycogen synthase, which inactivates it. The result is net glycogen breakdown with synthesis switched off, avoiding a futile cycle.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy develops severe painful cramps in his thigh muscles after a short sprint, and his urine turns dark brown. An ischaemic forearm exercise test produces no rise in venous lactate, and his fasting blood glucose is normal. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?

distractorRationale.a: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency causes fasting hypoglycaemia and hepatomegaly, not isolated exercise cramps with normal glucose.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: without muscle phosphorylase glycogen cannot feed glycolysis during exercise, so energy is short, lactate does not rise and muscle breakdown causes myoglobinuria.
distractorRationale.c: Debranching enzyme deficiency mainly causes liver involvement with hypoglycaemia, and lactate rises normally.
distractorRationale.d: Acid maltase deficiency (Pompe) causes lysosomal glycogen storage with hypotonia or cardiomegaly, not exercise-induced cramps with absent lactate rise.

questions.explanation: Exercise-induced cramps, myoglobinuria, a flat lactate response and normal blood glucose together indicate that muscle cannot break down its own glycogen, which is McArdle disease (muscle phosphorylase deficiency). Liver enzymes are intact, so fasting glucose stays normal.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old with hepatomegaly becomes hypoglycaemic after a 4-hour gap between feeds. Intramuscular glucagon given in this state fails to raise the blood glucose, but plasma lactate rises sharply. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Glucose-6-phosphate cannot be converted to free glucose, so it is diverted to glycolysis and lactate
The liver lacks glycogen phosphorylase, so no glucose-1-phosphate is formed
Pyruvate carboxylase is inactive, so lactate cannot enter gluconeogenesis
Glucagon receptors are absent from the liver, so cAMP cannot rise

questions.correctOptionText: Glucose-6-phosphate cannot be converted to free glucose, so it is diverted to glycolysis and lactate

distractorRationale.a: Correct: both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis converge on glucose-6-phosphate, so a glucose-6-phosphatase defect blocks all glucose release and drives lactate production.
distractorRationale.b: If phosphorylase were absent, glucagon would also fail, but lactate would not rise sharply and the block would be earlier in the pathway.
distractorRationale.c: Inactive pyruvate carboxylase would block conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate, but lactate rising despite glucagon points to a block at the last step.
distractorRationale.d: Absent glucagon receptors would not cause lactate to surge; the glucagon signal acts normally and the defect lies downstream.

questions.explanation: Glycogenolysis (via glucose-6-phosphate) and gluconeogenesis both end at glucose-6-phosphatase. When it is deficient (type I glycogen storage disease), glucose-6-phosphate accumulates and is pushed through glycolysis to lactate, which also cannot be used to form free glucose, so glucagon fails to raise glucose.

questions.stem: True or false: in humans, even-chain fatty acids can be converted to a net gain of glucose through gluconeogenesis.
questions.explanation: Acetyl-CoA from even-chain fatty acid oxidation loses both carbons as CO2 in the citric acid cycle, so no net oxaloacetate and therefore no net glucose is formed. Glycerol from triacylglycerol, lactate and glucogenic amino acids are the usable precursors.

questions.stem: A fasting patient has 72 g of liver glycogen. Whole-body glucose use is 7.5 g per hour, of which gluconeogenesis supplies 1.5 g per hour. Assuming the rest comes entirely from liver glycogen and rates stay constant, how many hours until the liver glycogen is exhausted?
questions.explanation: Glycogenolysis must supply the demand not met by gluconeogenesis: 7.5 - 1.5 = 6.0 g per hour. Dividing the store by this rate gives 72 / 6.0 = 12 hours, after which gluconeogenesis must increase to prevent hypoglycaemia.

questions.stem: In the Cori cycle, muscle converts one glucose to 2 lactate with a net gain of 2 ATP. The liver then converts 2 lactate back to one glucose, consuming 4 ATP and 2 GTP (each GTP counted as one ATP equivalent). What is the net number of ATP equivalents consumed by the body for each glucose cycled?
questions.explanation: The liver spends 4 ATP + 2 GTP = 6 ATP equivalents, while muscle gains only 2 ATP. The net cost is 6 - 2 = 4 ATP equivalents per glucose cycled, which is why the Cori cycle transfers energy cost from muscle to liver and wastes energy overall.

questions.stem: Explain how glucagon and insulin reciprocally regulate hepatic glycogen metabolism, naming the second messenger and the key enzymes involved, and state the metabolic result of each.
markingGuide: Glucagon binds a Gs-coupled receptor, activating adenylyl cyclase and raising cAMP, which activates protein kinase A
Protein kinase A activates phosphorylase kinase, which phosphorylates and activates glycogen phosphorylase
Glycogen synthase is phosphorylated and inactivated, so synthesis is switched off
Net effect of glucagon: glycogenolysis and release of glucose in the fasting state
Insulin activates protein phosphatase-1, which dephosphorylates synthase (active) and phosphorylase (inactive)
Net effect of insulin: glycogen synthesis and storage in the fed state
Reciprocal control avoids a futile cycle of simultaneous synthesis and breakdown
questions.explanation: The two hormones act through opposite phosphorylation states: glucagon, via cAMP and protein kinase A, phosphorylates enzymes so that phosphorylase is on and synthase is off. Insulin activates phosphatase activity so that the reverse holds, which ensures that breakdown and synthesis are never both maximal at once.

questions.stem: Contrast type I (von Gierke) and type V (McArdle) glycogen storage disease by naming the enzyme defect, the tissue affected, and explaining why one causes fasting hypoglycaemia whereas the other does not.
markingGuide: Type I: glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency in liver and kidney
Type V: muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency
Only liver (and kidney) can release free glucose into blood because only they express glucose-6-phosphatase
In type I, both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis end at glucose-6-phosphate, so fasting glucose cannot be maintained: severe hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis and hyperuricaemia
In type V, muscle glycogen is a private fuel store for the muscle itself and does not supply blood glucose, so fasting glucose is normal
Type V presents with exercise intolerance, cramps and myoglobinuria with no rise in lactate on ischaemic exercise
questions.explanation: The location of the enzyme determines the phenotype: the liver exports glucose, so a liver defect causes hypoglycaemia, whereas muscle glycogen only fuels muscle contraction, so a muscle phosphorylase defect causes exercise intolerance without hypoglycaemia. In type I the shared final step of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis is blocked, which explains the lactic acidosis and hyperuricaemia too.
